Train a two-tower retriever so user/context embeddings can query an ANN index of video embeddings. Build labels from logged exposure and meaningful engagement; unexposed videos are unlabeled, not proven dislikes. In-batch and sampled negatives make training feasible, but sampling distributions and false negatives must be accounted for when interpreting scores.

Retrieve a diverse union of personalized, subscribed, fresh, and exploration candidates. A richer ranker uses interaction features unavailable to the retrieval dot product. MMoE can share experts while allowing task-specific gates for clicks, watch quality, and satisfaction; it does not automatically resolve conflicting objectives. Calibrate outcome heads before utility combination.

Version user/video encoders and indexes together, and refresh new-video representations without requiring historical clicks. Log propensities on randomized exposure where practical to study selection bias. Measure retrieval recall separately from ranking quality; a reranker cannot recover absent candidates. Online guardrails include negative feedback, diversity, latency, and long-term satisfaction. This is a proposed architecture, not a claim about YouTube’s current internal implementation.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** A two-tower score $s(u,i)=f(u)^Tg(i)$ enables precomputed item vectors and ANN candidate retrieval. A richer cross-feature ranker operates only on the shortlist. Measure candidate recall before ranking quality: the ranker cannot recover an excellent video that retrieval never supplied. Correct sampled-negative objectives according to their actual sampling distribution. [3](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://research.google/pubs/deep-neural-networks-for-youtube-recommendations/) and [2](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/system-design-for-discovery/).
